title: Making 60,000 Particles Feel Alive (TSL + WebGPU)

So, before break down this effect, here's the general pipeline behind it. We start [music] with a 3D model, but the model itself is never directly rendered. Instead, we sample its surface to generate around 60,000 particles. Those particles are rendered using an instanced mesh, basically one sphere rendered thousands of times directly on the GPU. Then, inside a TSL shader, we handle all the lighting, noise deformation, and mouse interactions entirely in JavaScript. Finally, everything goes through post-processing, adding bloom to create the final look. So, with that foundation in place, let's start by turning a 3D model into particles. The first question is, how do you turn a 3D model into a cloud of particles that actually respects its shape? To achieve that, instead of rendering the GLB, we will iterate through each triangle of its mesh. Each of these gets a number of sample points proportional to its area. The result is a uniform distribution across the surface. This is what the raw sampling looks like. No lighting or effects. Just density. Every dot is one particle. But position alone isn't enough. If we only stored where each particle is, the whole cloud would look flat. To give the particle object volume, each sample also captures the surface normal of the GLB at that point. That normal is what tells the shader which way the surface is facing. And from that, we can compute lighting and shadow. That's what makes it read as a three-dimensional form instead of a flat silhouette. These normals will drive the lighting in the next section. And they also control the direction of the noise displacement, but that's coming up. At this point, we have the particles on the surface and normals that give the overall shape some volume. But we can push it further. Instead of rendering each particle as a flat point sprite, we're using actual sphere geometry per particle. The difference is significant. This is what separates a particle cloud that looks like a texture painted on a surface >> [music] >> from one that feels like it has real physical mass. For these purposes, we don't need a sphere with a lot of geometry to fulfill its purpose. This way, we save performance without [music] losing much visually. Now, let's look at the lighting. No color, just raw luminance. This is computed entirely in [music] the shader without scene lights or shadow maps. This is wrapped diffuse lighting. Traditional Lambert lighting creates a very hard fall off. Once the normal turns away from the light, it drops straight into darkness. The wrap parameter changes that. It pushes light slightly into the shadow side, giving the particles a much softer holographic response. The first light defines the top surfaces and the primary shape. For the second one, its job is to gently fill the shadow side. Together they create a full tonal range without anything collapsing into pure black. So now every particle has position, normal, and lighting. But it's still static. Now let's [music] make it move. Before continuing, if you're finding this video helpful, please leave a like and consider subscribing for more free resources [music] like this. Also, check out the other resources already available. With that said, let's continue with the particle animation. This is the noise field that drives the entire animation. Every particle is sampling a 3D fractal noise function at its world position. The brighter the particle, [music] the higher the noise value at that point. You can see it's not random per particle. It's a smooth continuous wave that flows through the whole volume. This coherence is what makes the displacement feel organic rather than chaotic. The scale value controls the frequency of the noise. At low values, you [music] get one broad wave moving across the entire figure. As the scale increases, the pattern breaks into tighter and finer detail. And this isn't just a single layer of noise. We're stacking multiple octaves together. Each one finer and slightly faster than the last. That's where the fractal look comes from. Now here's the important part. When we apply the displacement, the noise doesn't move particles in some fixed world [music] direction. Instead, the noise value gets multiplied by each particle's surface normal. So, every particle moves outward relative to its own surface orientation. That's why the silhouette remains readable even at high amplitudes because the motion still follows the underlying geometry. Back in the full render, that's the displacement you're seeing. The same noise field, now driving 60,000 particles per frame, entirely on the GPU in TSL. Now that we've added life to the particles, let's make them interactive for the user. We will use a second layer so that the particles respond when [music] moving the cursor over the model. Each particle checks its distance to the cursor in world space. >> [music] >> If it falls within the influence radius, it gets pushed outward away from the cursor position. The push strength and radius are both tunable, so you can go from a subtle ripple to a full scatter. But, they don't just snap back. Each particle runs a spring damper simulation on the CPU. A stiffness and damping value that controls how quickly and smoothly it returns to its resting position on the surface. This is what makes the interaction feel physical rather than scripted. On top of the displacement, there's a two-layer glow system. The first layer is passive. It's always on wherever the cursor is. Particles near the cursor emit a soft halo based purely on proximity. The second layer is active. It's driven by how fast the cursor is moving. The faster you move, the brighter the trail. When you stop, the energy decays [music] on its own curve, independent of the spring physics. So far, every system we've seen runs on a single model. But, the effect supports live model switching, and the transition between them is part of the design. When a new GLB loads, the particles don't jump to their new positions. Instead, the system runs a three-phase state machine. First, the current shape deforms outward. Particles drift away from the surface using the noise field. Then, they morph. Each particle travels directly from its current position to its target position on the new model. Finally, they reform. The noise fades back in and the new shape settles. The morph itself is driven by a single progress uniform on the GPU. Every particle interpolates linearly between its source and target position. No simulation, no physics. Pure lerp on the shader. Particles that travel the longest distance glow the brightest. The further a particle has to move, the more light it emits during the transition. The deform phase uses the same noise mask that drives the animation. It controls which particles leave the surface first, creating an organic, non-uniform dissolve rather than everything moving at once. The core system [music] is done.
